Back around 2000-2003, before Reddit existed, I spent a lot of my time on Slashdot. At the time, Microsoft was an avowed enemy of open source. Certainly it could be argued that it still is, but outwardly at least it has warmed up to it a lot. By contrast, in those days, Microsoft's attitude toward it was something like ExxonMobil's attitude toward global warming. MS execs were making strident public statements to the effect that open source was silly, a failed software philosophy.

Consequently, Microsoft was hated by the open source community, and there was lots of navel gazing about whether 2001 or 2002 or 2003 would finally be The Year of the Linux Desktop, when people would finally give up Windows en masse. Lots of distributions were trying hard to become more user-friendly and Windows-like in order to usher in and profit from this golden age. I remember one particularly ambitious attempt to create a Windows look-alike. It was called Lindows until MS sued the company and forced it to change it's name to Linspire. I remember my university had a small but dedicated LUG (Linux User Group) that passed out installation CDs like Gospel tracts in the lobby of the engineering building.

Of course, it eventually all petered out, and "Year of the Linux Desktop" became something of a bitter running joke.

But now it's back! Young, idealistic people are once again optimistic about the future of Linux on the desktop.

Putting aside the inconvenient fact that people have been pissed off at Microsoft before (Windows ME, Windows 8) but failed to flee to Linux in any significant numbers, maybe their optimism isn't unfounded. This may indeed be the best shot Linux has had for a while. Not only has MS introduced spying into recent versions of Windows, but Linux has addressed quite a few of the usability challenges it faced back then. Software repositories and package managers have saved people from dependency hell, a term which a lot of you young folks probably have never even heard or worried about. Virtually all hardware is now supported at least a bit. To me, the GUIs that ship with most distros still seem amateurish compared to Windows and Mac, which have been meticulously worked over by armies of professional researchers and designers, but they've absolutely closed the gap quite a bit from the late 90s/early 2000s.

So, why not? Maybe Linux on the desktop will finally succeed.

Except, here's the thing. In the early 2000s, usability may have prevented a few ideologically minded and technically sophisticated people from making the switch, but I don't think it's what was holding back the masses. Then as now, Linux was perfectly usable for most of what ordinary people do with their desktop computers.

The issue is that Linux has never offered any advantage over Windows or Mac that the vast majority of people actually care about. Fifteen years ago, the rallying cry was open software philosophy. That was a non-starter. The average person didn't understand or care about open source philosophy.

Now it's about privacy. Switch to Linux to avoid being spied on. This too will fail. Our society collectively yawned after being told that the government is essentially recording their phone calls. It is supremely naive to believe that practically anyone will sit up and care that Microsoft is monitoring them, too.

So, yeah. The enthusiasm is cute and it reminds me of myself when I was in college, fighting the man by dual-booting, spending what little folding money I had on peripherals that were Linux compatible, and spending my abundant free-time tinkering. And although I realize I'm wasting my energy by saying so, I'll say it anyway. Find another cause to fight, something else to get worked up and outraged about. You are wasting your time on this. There will never be a Year of the Linux Desktop unless Microsoft adopts Linux the way Apple adopted BSD.
